clue.text: Flowering plant envisaged in a dream

definitions.meaning: a garden perennial with ladder-like leaves and blue flowers bears this name
in Genesis the patriarch dreams of a stairway reaching up to heaven

explanation.definitionFit: Both the cottage-garden plant (Polemonium) and the biblical stairway seen in a vision carry this name.

clue.text: Caretaker sees rubbish piled up after Bank Holiday

indicators.note: after places the upturned rubbish behind the holiday

parts.note: New Year's Day, 1 January, is a public holiday, written JAN I with I as the Roman one

indicators.note: in a down clue, piled up means the word is stacked from the bottom, read upwards

parts.note: rot means nonsense or rubbish

explanation.surface: A building's caretaker finds refuse heaped up following a public holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: New Year's Day, 1 January, is a UK bank holiday, written JAN I; 'piled up' reads the rubbish upwards, and 'after' places it behind the date.
explanation.definitionFit: A janitor is the person employed to look after a building, a synonym for caretaker.

clue.text: Smoke rising, sad, timeless

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the letters read upwards
less the time, so the abbreviation T for time is removed

parts.note: tragic means sad or calamitous

explanation.surface: Someone's mournful cigarette smoke drifts up in an eternal moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'timeless' removes T from TRAGIC, leaving RAGIC, and 'rising' reads it upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A cigar is something you smoke, so the noun smoke can stand for one.

clue.text: Study with window, perhaps, where old prisoners settled

parts.note: botany is the study of plants
a bay is a kind of window, as in bay window

explanation.surface: A scholar with a window seat, in a place where former convicts made homes.
explanation.walkthrough: Botany Bay, near Sydney, was the name long attached to the penal colony to which British convicts were transported.
explanation.definitionFit: Botany Bay in New South Wales gave its name to the destination of transported British convicts.

clue.text: Such an easy source of funds, with one pound left at first

definitions.text: Such an easy source of funds

indicators.note: at first puts the left letter at the front of the word

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
a quid is slang for a pound sterling

explanation.surface: Describing a ready source of money, with a single pound left over to start.
explanation.walkthrough: Liquid assets are cash or things readily turned into cash, hence an easy source of funds; 'at first' puts L ahead of I and QUID.
explanation.definitionFit: Liquid assets are ones readily converted to cash, so such assets give an easy source of money.

clue.text: Calibre of network girl set up

indicators.note: in a down clue, set up means the whole run is raised, read upwards

parts.note: rete is an anatomical term for a network of nerves or vessels
a maid is a girl

explanation.surface: Assessing the quality of a broadcasting network that a young woman established.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set up' turns the whole of RETE + MAID upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The calibre of a gun is the internal diameter of its barrel.

clue.text: One over fifty, diving in river, being forced to leave

indicators.note: diving in means plunging inside the river

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon

indicators.note: in a down clue, over puts the one on top of the fifty

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
L is the Roman numeral fifty

explanation.surface: A man past fifty dives into a river as he is driven out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'diving in' puts I over L inside EXE, a river in Devon.
explanation.definitionFit: Exile is enforced absence from one's country, the state of being made to leave it.

clue.text: Competition involving crowd puller — no second half?

indicators.note: involving in the sense of entangling, so the letters are tangled together

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: without its second half, the word puller loses its last three letters

explanation.surface: A contest featuring a big attraction, but without a second half of play?
explanation.walkthrough: 'no second half' trims PULLER to PUL; 'involving' tangles CROWD with it.
explanation.definitionFit: The World Cup is the international football tournament, the best-known sporting competition.

clue.text: One of the distinguished people who try desperately

indicators.note: desperately suggests the letters are thrown about wildly

explanation.surface: A notable figure among those who make frantic efforts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'desperately' rearranges WHO TRY.
explanation.definitionFit: A worthy is a notable or eminent person, often used of local dignitaries.

clue.text: Time to say one's piece

indicators.note: to say means the word is spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: a knight is a chess piece belonging to one player

explanation.surface: The moment has come to speak your mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one's piece' suggests having one's say, but it is a chess knight, which sounds the same without its silent K.
explanation.definitionFit: Night is a period of time, the hours of darkness.

clue.text: Low Sunday, when cathedral bellringer puts in an appearance

definitions.meaning: the first Sunday after Easter takes a Latin name from the opening words of its introit
the hunchback who rings the bells of Notre-Dame in Victor Hugo's novel

explanation.definitionFit: The Sunday after Easter is named from the introit beginning Quasi modo geniti, and Hugo's bellringer was found on that day.

clue.text: In ancient city, woman is subject to oppression

indicators.note: in places the woman and is inside the city

parts.note: Tyre was an ancient Phoenician city
Ann is a woman's name

explanation.surface: In an old city a woman is being crushed under tyranny.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' puts the woman and 'is' inside the city; 'subject to oppression' is the definition, not a description of the woman.
explanation.definitionFit: To tyrannise is to rule cruelly, to subject people to oppression.

clue.text: Approval of story about Conservative setback

indicators.note: setback read as set back, so the letters run backwards
about means the story goes around the abbreviation

parts.note: a tale is a story

explanation.surface: Endorsement of an account of a Tory party reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts C inside TALE to make TALCE, and 'setback' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Eclat is brilliant success or acclaim, the applause that marks approval.

clue.text: Rob him with violence, to get diamonds

indicators.note: violence wrenches the letters out of order

explanation.surface: Mug a man forcefully to steal his jewels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with violence' rearranges ROB HIM.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhombi are diamond shapes, plural of rhombus, an equal-sided parallelogram.

clue.text: Source of arsenic, or allspice, mostly

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: mostly means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: pimento is another name for allspice

explanation.surface: A kitchen query: is that poison from arsenic, or from a spice?
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' drops the last O from PIMENTO.
explanation.definitionFit: Orpiment is a yellow mineral, arsenic trisulphide, mined as an ore of arsenic.

clue.text: County losing millions in filthy state

parts.note: Kent is an English county in the south-east

indicators.note: losing millions removes M, the abbreviation for millions

parts.note: mucky means filthy

explanation.surface: An English shire, its fortune gone, ends up in a dirty condition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing millions' removes M from MUCKY. KENT is a county in south-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: Kentucky is one of the states of the USA.

clue.text: Will he finish the order, thanks to one bank?

parts.note: ta is informal British for thanks
I is the Roman numeral one
a bank is a lender of money

explanation.surface: Will he complete the purchase, with credit from a single bank?
explanation.walkthrough: The order is cricket's batting order: a tail-ender bats near the end, a weak batsman.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a tail-ender is one of the last batsmen in the batting order.

clue.text: At heart, dozing, beggar mourns deaths in Babylonian temple

indicators.note: at heart takes the central pair of letters from each word

explanation.surface: A sleepy beggar grieves for the dead in an ancient Mesopotamian shrine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At heart' takes the middle two letters of each of the four words: ZI, GG, UR, AT.
explanation.definitionFit: A ziggurat is a stepped pyramid temple of ancient Mesopotamia such as Babylon.

clue.text: Shortness of breath? Remedy said to be found in far East

indicators.note: to be found in places the remedy inside the continent

parts.note: Asia is the continent lying far to the east

indicators.note: said means the word is heard, spelt differently

parts.note: a fix is a remedy for a problem

explanation.surface: Breathless? A cure is said to be available in the Orient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'said' means the remedy is spelt as it sounds, with PH for F and Y for I; 'to be found in' sets it inside the continent. The question mark flags asphyxia as an extreme lack of breath.
explanation.definitionFit: Asphyxia is suffocation from lack of oxygen, an extreme shortage of breath.

clue.text: Deeply aroused, a man 'upset me

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset turns the man's name upside down

parts.note: Alf is a man's name
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone confesses passion: a man has thrown them into turmoil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns only the man's name upwards, and it sits between A and ME; the apparent anagram of 'a man' is a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: Aflame describes someone burning with passion, intensely stirred.

clue.text: Allow little devil to enter — he's not easily got rid of

definitions.text: he's not easily got rid of

indicators.note: to enter means the devil goes into the other word

parts.note: let means allow
an imp is a little devil

explanation.surface: Let a small demon in and you will never shake him off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to enter' puts the devil inside the word for allow. A limpet clings to rocks, hence a person hard to shake off.
explanation.definitionFit: A limpet clings tenaciously to rock, so the word figuratively describes someone who sticks around.

clue.text: Plays in what heat remains

indicators.note: in means the letters sit within the following words

explanation.surface: Dramas set in whatever warmth is left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points to the run inside 'whaT HEAT REmains'.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatre means drama collectively, plays as an art form or body of work.

clue.text: Servant attending a dance

parts.note: a valet is a manservant

explanation.surface: A manservant escorting someone to a ball.
explanation.walkthrough: The valeta is an old-time ballroom dance in waltz time.
explanation.definitionFit: The valeta is an old-time round dance in triple time, popular in British ballrooms.

clue.text: Proposition girl after end of ball

indicators.note: after puts the girl behind the final letter
end of takes the final letter of ball

parts.note: Emma is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A suitor's proposal to a young woman at the close of a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'end of' takes L from ball, and 'after' puts EMMA behind it. 'Proposition' looks like a pass at the girl, but a lemma is a logical proposition.
explanation.definitionFit: A lemma is a subsidiary proposition proved as a step towards a theorem.

clue.text: In the past, king imprisoned for trouble-making

indicators.note: imprisoned means the king is locked inside

parts.note: ago means in the past
GR stands for Georgius Rex, King George

explanation.surface: Long ago a monarch was jailed for stirring up strife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'imprisoned' locks the king inside the word for in the past. Aggro is British slang for aggressive, troublesome behaviour.
explanation.definitionFit: Aggro is informal British slang for aggressive behaviour or deliberately caused trouble.

clue.text: Note profound split about exercising source of rumour

parts.note: G is a musical note

indicators.note: about means the split goes around the exercise

parts.note: a ravine is a deep cleft in the land
PE, physical education, is exercising

explanation.surface: Note a deep division over physical training, where gossip begins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps the deep split round the exercise, after the note; hearing something 'on the grapevine' means by rumour.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearing something on the grapevine means picking up gossip through informal channels, so it is a source of rumour.

clue.text: One business established on a resort island

indicators.note: in a down clue, established on means set on top of the next piece

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
biz is informal for business

explanation.surface: A single company set up on a holiday isle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'established on' puts I + BIZ above A in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Ibiza is a Balearic island in the Mediterranean known as a holiday resort.

clue.text: Animals go in here and emerge in a flap

indicators.note: a flap is a state of agitation, so the letters before it are stirred up

explanation.surface: Creatures enter this place and come out in a state of panic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flap' rearranges EMERGE IN A; the phrase 'in a flap' reads as panic, but 'in a' is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A menagerie is a collection of wild animals kept for exhibition, a place animals are housed.

clue.text: Tenor appears to be aimless

definitions.meaning: the tenor of a speech is its general meaning or gist
to move along without purpose, carried by events

explanation.definitionFit: Drift means both the gist of what is said and to wander along without purpose.

clue.text: Wordsworth, for instance, ate purée a lot, all mashed up

indicators.note: mashed up, like food, means the letters are pulped and reformed

explanation.surface: The great Romantic poet gorged himself on puréed food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mashed up' rearranges ATE PUREE A LOT; 'all' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: William Wordsworth held the office of Poet Laureate, so he is an example of one.
